sections.overview: This tiny migratory sandpiper breeds across northern Siberia and winters from Southeast Asia to Australia and New Zealand; in Japan it is mainly a passage migrant.
sections.identification: At about 14–15 cm, it is one of the smallest Calidris; in breeding plumage its rusty head and breast contrast with dark-spotted upperparts, while the short dark bill and legs help separate it from some similar stints.
sections.habitat: On passage and in winter it uses intertidal mudflats, sheltered estuaries and lagoons, but also sandy shores and occasionally inland lakes or flooded fields.
sections.diet: It probes shallow mud and water for small invertebrates, including worms, insects and crustaceans; plant material is also reported in some feeding accounts.
sections.behavior: Outside the breeding season it is highly gregarious, often feeding and roosting in dense flocks that may mingle with other small shorebirds.
sections.reproduction: It nests on northern tundra; the adults move south after breeding, following the East Asian–Australasian Flyway between Arctic nesting grounds and southern coastal wetlands.
sections.ecology: It shares the genus Calidris with the much larger Great Knot (C. tenuirostris), described in the neighbouring bestiary entry; their contrasting size and feeding niches make the comparison useful, though both depend on healthy tidal flats during migration.
sections.conservation: BirdLife’s 2024 assessment classifies it as Near Threatened, reflecting continuing declines associated with pressure on intertidal habitat along the flyway.
